Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette: At 41, Mira was on a late-night tour bus, the hum of the engine a familiar lullaby, when a sudden, crushing shortness of breath hit her like a wave. The ambulance ride was a blur of white lights and frantic murmurs, the smell of antiseptic seeping into her nose. In the emergency room she was diagnosed with a massive pulmonary embolism that had nearly claimed her life. The doctors' rapid blood draws, the needles that pricked her skin, and the constant hiss of oxygen masks left her with a visceral memory that she could not erase. Even months later, the mere scent of hospital disinfectant can make her gasp, and a sudden feeling of breathlessness can strike when she is halfway through a rehearsal, her body reacting before she can even think. Her sense of inadequacy grew in the quiet hours after the event. Mira began to view herself as a "bad coper," convinced that she had failed to protect her own life. She told herself she deserved the suffering she now endured, a self-punishment that left her feeling powerless. Those harsh, self-critical thoughts pushed her into a loop of counterfactual thinking-she would have been safer had she never gotten sick, had she taken better care of herself. The negative appraisals that framed her identity as inadequate and ineffective fed directly into the maladaptive strategies she used to cope, turning her internal criticism into a self-fulfilling pattern of self-blame and regret. The persistent threat of a recurrence loomed over her every waking moment. At night, Mira would wake with her heart pounding, checking her phone for news of medical appointments or the temperature in the room, convinced that a sudden collapse could happen again. Her body would tense, her skin would clamour for air, even though no obvious danger was present. That threat, unrelenting and invisible, drove her to avoid any medical cues-she declined routine check-ups, left early from the dentist, and refused to carry a portable pulse oximeter that her doctor had suggested. Each avoidance was a conscious decision to keep the feeling of threat at bay, yet it reinforced her pattern of counterfactual rumination and self-punishment. The sense that her body could betray her at any time made her retreat further from the very interventions that might safeguard her health. Because the threat persisted, Mira's view of herself deepened into a story of failure. She could not trust that she would do the right thing when danger seemed inevitable, and she began to doubt her own judgment in every decision. The belief that she was inadequate-unable to protect herself, unable to respond appropriately-solidified her negative appraisal of her own competence. In turn, these appraisals fed back into the maladaptive cycle: the more she doubted herself, the more she sought to avoid anything that might remind her of her frailty, and the more she believed she was doomed to repeat the tragedy. The same sense of threat also set off the specific triggers that punctuate her daily life. Every time she hears the faint smell of bleach on a travel bag, she feels a tightening in her chest, a flash of the hospital corridor's sterile scent. When a friend mentions a new health policy and suggests a quick blood test, Mira's breath hitches; she feels as if a needle might strike her skin at any moment. Even the simple act of filling her instrument case-an action that requires her to bend close to a metal box that sometimes rattles-can send her body into a state of pre-emptive tension, before her mind even registers the routine. These triggers-breathlessness, smell, and medical procedures-are not merely reminders; they are the physical manifestations of the threat that has taken root in her psyche. Mira's current distress culminated when a rehearsal turned into a nightmare. Midway through a piece, she suddenly felt her chest tighten so severely that she could not continue. She slipped from her guitar, the sound of the strings breaking reverberating through the small studio. She lay there, coughing and gasping, alone and terrified that the panic would never end. It was then she realized that her avoidance of medical care, her constant self-blame, and her nightly checks had all led to this moment of crisis. The fear that her body might collapse again, coupled with her conviction that she was powerless, forced her to finally seek help. She now hopes that a clinician can untangle the web of self-critical thoughts and physical triggers that have kept her in a state of perpetual alert, and she fears that, without intervention, she will continue to miss the music she loves and the life she once felt capable of living.
